newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac fails to stifle election, reshuffle rumours.
newsitem.headline: Chirac fails to stifle election, reshuffle rumours.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac failed on Thursday to stamp out rumours of a snap election or a cabinet reshuffle after denials backhandedly confirmed he was considering some type of initiative.

"Shhh. The president is reflecting", the left-leaning daily Liberation said in a front-page headline. The conservative daily Le Figaro went so far as to say that any dissolution of parliament would probably mean a two-stage vote on June 1 and 8.
Chirac might be tempted to call an election, bringing forward a vote for the National Assembly set for March 1998, to secure a renewed centre-right majority for the rest of his seven-year term.
A less dramatic cabinet reshuffle might help heal rifts in the fractious ruling coalition.

An early election "is not impossible", said Pierre Mazeaud, a leading parliamentarian in the Gaullist party founded by Chirac. "It is part of the solutions that seem to be under consideration at the moment."

"One may consider it necessary to get a second wind," he told France Inter radio on Thursday. Economic growth has picked up slightly, as has the popularity of Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe in opinion polls this year.

An election might also allow Chirac to seize the initiative on European integration and ensure that campaigning does not coincide with European Union debate early next year on which countries make the grade for a single currency from 1999.

Chirac has so far failed to quash the speculation. An official source at his office said on Wednesday that rumours of a reshuffle or early election were baseless but added: "The president has time on his hands for reflection."

If Chirac did call a snap election, it would be the first time in France's 39-year-old Fifth Republic that a president has dissolved the Assembly without a major crisis brewing. The ruling coalition controls 80 percent of the Assembly's seats.
A reshuffle would be more mundane -- Prime Minister Alain Juppe's two-year-old government has had one reshuffle already, in November 1995.
Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure dismissed talk of an early election or a reshuffle as "bar-room speculation" but said that only the president had the power to decide such issues.
"When this type of decision is taken, in general, if it is to work properly, it's best to have a surprise effect," he told RTL radio.
Serge July, publisher of Liberation, said the need to boost European integration was the only argument Chirac could convincingly invoke to dissolve parliament and seek a renewed majority.
July said he could imagine Chirac announcing early elections by arguing: "I need a legislature and a majority to create Europe and so that France can be a leader in this new political entity".

The opposition Socialist Party, still convalescing after its rout in the last elections in 1993, has ridiculed the idea of an election justified by Europe, saying the timetable of the EU's Maastricht Treaty was set years ago.
Socialist leaders point out that France has already ratified the treaty in a referendum, the only EU nation apart from Denmark to have consulted the electorate directly.

Lamassoure, who is also budget minister, denied speculation that Chirac might justify an election by arguing that a special new bout of austerity is needed to ensure that France meets strict fiscal criteria for a single currency.
"We have no budgetary problems at the moment," he said.
